title: Kissing the leper
hookLine: Francis writes that what was bitter became sweet

lines: OUT OF THE CLOISTER, ONTO THE ROAD.
cards: Francis of Assisi left a short text now called his Testament, looking back at how it all began. A reader might expect a vision, a voice from heaven, a dramatic call. Instead he starts with his stomach.
When he was living in sin, he says, the very sight of lepers was too bitter for him to bear.

That's where the story of the Franciscans opens: not with a great deed, but with a man who couldn't stand to look at certain people. Benedict's cloister is behind us now; this is the road, and the friars.

teach.h: THE LORD LED ME AMONG THEM.
teach.b: Here's what Francis says happened. The Lord himself led him among the lepers, and he showed them mercy.

teach.h: WHAT WAS BITTER WAS TURNED TO SWEETNESS.
teach.b: And when he left them, what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, of soul and of body. Then, he says, he waited a little while, and left the world.
A few lines, and in his own telling, the hinge of his whole life. Notice what he doesn't say. There's no kiss.

teach.h: THE KISS COMES FROM THE BIOGRAPHERS.
teach.b: The kiss comes from the stories his early biographers told. In their telling, Francis is riding near Assisi when he meets a leper on the road. Everything in him wants to turn the horse around.
Instead he gets down, gives the man money, and kisses his hand, and the leper kisses him back. In some versions he then goes to the place where lepers lived and serves them there.
Francis's own spare account, and the vivid scene the biographers drew: both land on the same turn.
Look at who does what in the Testament. Francis doesn't say he conquered his disgust. He says the Lord led him.

teach.h: THE FEELING CAME AFTER THE MERCY.
teach.b: The change in his feelings came after the mercy, not before it. He didn't wait to feel sweetness before he went; the bitterness changed on the way out. That suggests the feeling of revulsion isn't a verdict.
It can be the doorway. In the gospels Jesus touches a leper before he heals him.

how: Franciscans tell the story of the leper as the start of Francis's conversion, and Franciscan friars and sisters still serve the sick and the poor in hospitals, shelters and missions.

o: a healing miracle Francis worked on a sick man's skin
a vow Francis took to live in a leper colony for life
Francis's turning point: mercy shown where he felt disgust

games.q: the leper story — tap the pairs.
p: too bitter to bear, at first

s: in his Testament, Francis describes kissing a leper
he says he showed lepers mercy. the kiss comes from his early biographers.
Francis says the Lord led him among the lepers
in his telling, he didn't conquer his disgust; he was led.
Francis felt sweetness first, and then went to the lepers
the bitterness turned to sweetness after he showed them mercy.

games.q: you're Francis, riding near Assisi. a leper is on the road ahead, and everything in you wants to turn the horse around. what do you do?
o: toss him a coin from the saddle.
get down, give him money, and kiss his hand.
games.why: in the biographers' telling he dismounts, gives the man money and kisses him. in his own Testament, he simply says the bitter became sweet.

practice: Let one thing come to mind that makes you pull back, not something dangerous, just a call you've avoided or a person you steer around, and notice where the feeling sits in your body without arguing with it.

Then picture yourself doing it anyway, gently, the way Francis got down from his horse, and see whether the picture changes the feeling at all. If you pray, ask to be led, the way Francis says he was.

wordCard.voice: Kissing the leper. The turning point Francis described in his Testament: what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness, once he showed mercy. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: sweetness, the word Francis's Testament uses for what the bitterness became.

carryVoice: Your line: bitter became sweet. It began with being led, not with feeling brave. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.work: The Writings of Saint Francis of Assisi
